Case study: scoring a CDISC pilot for submission readiness

Source: vignettes/case-study-cdisc-pilot.Rmd
case-study-cdisc-pilot.Rmd

You have run Pinnacle 21, checked your Define-XML, and looked over the datasets. The output is a few hundred findings spread across a dozen tools. The question the study team actually asks is simpler than any single report answers: are we ready to file?

This is what the Submission Confidence Index (SCI) is for. It takes a table of evidence and returns one number between 0 and 100, plus a decision band, plus a breakdown of where the number comes from. Here we walk a realistic CDISC pilot study through it, using the example evidence that ships with r4subdata.

library(r4subscore)
library(r4subdata)

The evidence

evidence_pharma is a validation run for a CDISC pilot study: 250 findings from tools like Pinnacle 21, spread across the four readiness pillars.

ev <- evidence_pharma
nrow(ev)
#> [1] 250
table(ev$indicator_domain, ev$result)
#>            
#>             fail na pass warn
#>   quality     26 14   55   25
#>   risk         6  2   24    7
#>   trace        9  1   29    8
#>   usability    8  3   26    7

Each row is one check against one asset, carrying a severity and a result. That is the whole contract. Any tool that can write this shape feeds the score.

The score

Three calls take the evidence to a number: indicators, pillars, then the composite index.

ind <- compute_indicator_scores(ev)
ps  <- compute_pillar_scores(ev)
sci <- compute_sci(ps)

sci
#> ℹ Submission Confidence Index: 44.4
#> ℹ Decision Band: "high_risk"
#> ℹ   quality: 39.6 (weight: 0.35)
#> ℹ   trace: 43.9 (weight: 0.25)
#> ℹ   risk: 49.9 (weight: 0.25)
#> ℹ   usability: 47.2 (weight: 0.15)

The pillar scores show where the study stands on each front before they are weighted together.

ps
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   pillar    pillar_score n_indicators weight
#>   <chr>            <dbl>        <int>  <dbl>
#> 1 quality          0.396            8   0.35
#> 2 trace            0.439            4   0.25
#> 3 risk             0.499            3   0.25
#> 4 usability        0.472            3   0.15

Where the score comes from

A single number is only useful if you can open it up. sci_explain() reports each pillar’s contribution and, more usefully, ranks the indicators dragging the score down.

expl <- sci_explain(ev)
expl$pillar_contributions
#> # A tibble: 4 × 6
#>   pillar    pillar_score n_indicators weight contribution  loss
#>   <chr>            <dbl>        <int>  <dbl>        <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 quality          0.396            8   0.35         13.9  21.1
#> 2 trace            0.439            4   0.25         11    14  
#> 3 risk             0.499            3   0.25         12.5  12.5
#> 4 usability        0.472            3   0.15          7.1   7.9
head(expl$indicator_contributions, 8)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 6
#>   indicator_id     indicator_name     indicator_domain indicator_score  loss
#>   <chr>            <chr>              <chr>                      <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 R-HIGH-RPN       High RPN Item      risk                       0.323  5.64
#> 2 T-ORPHAN-VAR     Orphan Variable    trace                      0.292  4.43
#> 3 T-TRACE-LEVEL    Traceability Level trace                      0.362  3.98
#> 4 R-MITIGATION-GAP Mitigation Gap     risk                       0.527  3.94
#> 5 Q-TYPE-MISMATCH  Type Mismatch      quality                    0.259  3.24
#> 6 Q-FORMAT-ERR     Format Error       quality                    0.321  2.97
#> 7 R-OPEN-RISK      Open Risk          risk                       0.648  2.94
#> 8 T-AMBIGUOUS-MAP  Ambiguous Mapping  trace                      0.533  2.92
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: pct_of_total_loss <dbl>

The indicators at the top of that list are where remediation buys the most. A team can work the list from the top and watch the score move, rather than guessing which of 250 findings matter.

Is the score stable?

The default weights (quality 0.35, trace 0.25, risk 0.25, usability 0.15) are a choice, not a law. Before anyone leans on the number, it is worth asking how much it depends on that choice. sci_sensitivity_analysis() recomputes the SCI across a grid of alternative weightings.

grid <- data.frame(
  quality   = c(0.35, 0.50, 0.25, 0.40),
  trace     = c(0.25, 0.20, 0.30, 0.20),
  risk      = c(0.25, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30),
  usability = c(0.15, 0.10, 0.20, 0.10)
)

sci_sensitivity_analysis(ev, weight_grid = grid)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 7
#>   scenario quality trace  risk usability   SCI band     
#>      <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl> <chr>    
#> 1        1    0.35  0.25  0.25      0.15  44.4 high_risk
#> 2        2    0.5   0.2   0.2       0.1   43.3 high_risk
#> 3        3    0.25  0.3   0.25      0.2   45   high_risk
#> 4        4    0.4   0.2   0.3       0.1   44.3 high_risk

If the band holds across that grid, the readiness call is robust to the weighting. If it flips between bands, the honest reading is that the decision hangs on a judgment about which pillar matters most, and that judgment should be made explicitly rather than buried in a default.

What this answers

The SCI does not replace the underlying checks. It sits on top of them and answers the one question the checks cannot: taken together, how ready is this submission, and what would move the needle first. For a study team deciding whether to file, that is the number that matters.
